chunks.heading: Plans and prices at a glance
chunks.text: This sheet describes how Nimbus Platform is priced as of September 15, 2026. Nimbus is sold in four plans: Free, Starter, Pro and Enterprise. Every plan covers the core workspace, and the differences between them come down to capacity, limits, security controls and a few optional add-ons, which are described in the sections that follow. Prices are quoted per user per month, billed annually. The Free plan costs $0 and supports up to 3 users, which makes it a good fit for a very small team or for someone trying out a workspace before inviting colleagues. Starter is $9 per user per month. Pro is $24 per user per month.

chunks.heading: Plans and prices at a glance
chunks.text: Enterprise is sold on custom pricing, with a minimum of 50 users, so a quote is prepared for each customer after a conversation with our sales team. If you would rather pay month to month, monthly billing costs 20% more than annual billing. You can see which billing option your workspace uses by opening Settings, choosing Billing, and looking at the Billing cycle line under your current plan. Switching to annual billing is done from the same screen. This sheet replaces the pricing sheet effective March 1, 2026. Anything you purchased or quoted under that earlier sheet is covered by the transition notes later in this document, so please read those before assuming your price has changed.

chunks.heading: Storage, version history and devices
chunks.text: Capacity is the most visible difference between plans, and it is measured per user. Each person in your workspace receives their own allowance rather than drawing from one shared pool. The Free plan includes 5 GB per user. Starter includes 100 GB per user. Pro includes 1 TB per user, and Enterprise storage is unlimited. Version history controls how far back you can go when you need to restore an earlier copy of a file. To use it, open a file, select the History tab in the side panel, pick the version you want, and choose Restore. On the Free plan, versions are kept for 7 days.

chunks.heading: Storage, version history and devices
chunks.text: Starter keeps them for 30 days, and Pro keeps them for 180 days. Enterprise workspaces keep version history for 10 years, which suits teams with long retention needs. Once a version ages out of the window for your plan, it no longer appears in the History tab. Nimbus Sync, the desktop and mobile companion that keeps files available offline, limits the number of devices each user can connect. Free users can link 2 devices. Starter users can link 5, and Pro users can link 10. Enterprise users have no device limit. You can review and remove linked devices from your profile under the Devices section, which is useful when you replace a laptop or phone.

chunks.heading: Nimbus Gateway API limits
chunks.text: Nimbus Gateway is the API layer used to connect your workspace to other tools and internal scripts. Its limits apply to the workspace as a whole, not to individual users, so every integration and token in the workspace shares the same allowance. The first limit is the daily quota, which is the total number of API requests your workspace can make in a day. Free workspaces can make 1,000 requests. Starter workspaces can make 10,000. Pro workspaces can make 100,000, and Enterprise workspaces can make 1,000,000.

chunks.heading: Nimbus Gateway API limits
chunks.text: If your integrations regularly come close to the quota, it is worth reviewing whether they poll more often than they need to, or whether a higher plan is a better match for your usage. The second limit is the burst limit, which caps how many requests can arrive in a single second regardless of how much daily quota remains. Free workspaces are limited to 5 requests per second. Starter allows 20, Pro allows 100, and Enterprise allows 500.

chunks.heading: Nimbus Gateway API limits
chunks.text: A script that sends many calls in a tight loop can hit the burst limit well before it uses up its daily quota, so spacing requests out or queuing them usually resolves the problem. You can watch your current usage in the Gateway dashboard, under the Usage tab in the workspace settings.

chunks.heading: Security, administration and add-ons
chunks.text: Several security and administration features depend on your plan. Single sign-on (SSO) is included in Pro and Enterprise and works with both SAML 2.0 and OIDC identity providers. To set it up, an administrator opens Settings, selects Security, chooses Single sign-on, and follows the prompts to connect the identity provider. SCIM user provisioning, which lets your identity provider create and deactivate accounts automatically, is included in Enterprise only. Two-factor authentication is available on all plans, including Free. Individual users can turn it on from their profile, and we recommend doing so for every account that holds sensitive files.

chunks.heading: Security, administration and add-ons
chunks.text: Audit logs, which record administrative and sharing activity in the workspace, are included in Enterprise. Pro customers who need them can buy audit logs as an add-on for $3 per user per month. Starter and Free workspaces do not have an audit log option. Nimbus Analytics, our reporting product for usage and collaboration trends, is included in Pro and Enterprise. Starter customers can add it for $5 per user per month. It is not available on the Free plan. Add-ons are managed from Settings under Billing, where an administrator can switch them on or off for the workspace and see the effect on the next invoice.

chunks.heading: What changed from the March 1, 2026 sheet
chunks.text: If you are comparing this document with the earlier pricing, here is what is different from the March 1, 2026 pricing. The Pro price rose from $20 to $24 per user per month. Alongside that increase, single sign-on moved from Enterprise-only to Pro and Enterprise, so teams on Pro can now connect their identity provider without upgrading. Starter storage doubled from 50 GB to 100 GB per user, and the larger allowance applies to Starter workspaces automatically without any action from administrators. One change reduces what the entry plan offers: the Free plan user limit dropped from 5 users to 3 users.

chunks.heading: What changed from the March 1, 2026 sheet
chunks.text: Workspaces that are affected should review their member list under Settings and Members, and decide whether to remove users or move to a paid plan. Existing Pro customers keep $20 pricing until their first renewal after January 1, 2027. In practice, this means that if your Pro subscription renews before that date, you continue to pay the earlier rate, and the new $24 price applies at the first renewal that falls after it. Your invoice and the Billing screen show the rate that applies to you, so check them if you are unsure which one you are paying.

chunks.heading: Discounts and volume pricing
chunks.text: Nimbus publishes a small number of discounts, and they are described here so that you can tell what is available before you contact us. Registered nonprofits receive 30% off Starter and Pro. To apply, an administrator opens Settings, selects Billing, chooses Request a discount, and submits documentation showing the organization's registered status. Once the request is approved, the reduction appears on later invoices for the eligible plan. Accredited schools can use Pro free for up to 100 seats. The request follows the same route in the Billing screen, with accreditation details in place of nonprofit registration.

chunks.heading: Discounts and volume pricing
chunks.text: Seats beyond that allowance are not covered by the school offer, so larger institutions should speak with us about their needs. No other discounts are published. That means there are no standing promotions for startups, students, referrals or long-term commitments in this pricing, and support staff cannot add one to a self-serve plan. Volume pricing for Enterprise is set by contract. If your organization is considering Enterprise, our sales team will prepare a proposal based on your size and requirements, and the agreed terms are written into your order form rather than listed on this sheet.

chunks.heading: Plans and per-user pricing
chunks.text: This sheet describes how Nimbus Platform is priced and how to read the figures before you choose a plan. All per-user prices are quoted per user per month, billed annually, so the amount you see on the pricing page reflects an annual commitment rather than a month-to-month charge. The Free plan costs $0 and is intended for very small teams, supporting up to 5 users. It is a good place to evaluate the workspace before you invite anyone else. Starter is $9 per user per month, billed annually, and suits growing teams that need more room to work.

chunks.heading: Plans and per-user pricing
chunks.text: Pro is $20 per user per month, billed annually, and is aimed at organizations that rely on the platform every day. Enterprise is priced custom, so the figure depends on your agreement with the Nimbus sales team. Storage scales with the plan. Each Starter user receives 50 GB of storage, while each Pro user receives 1 TB. Because storage is allocated per user, adding a teammate to either plan increases your total capacity. Single sign-on (SSO) is included in Enterprise only. If your security team requires SSO, open Settings, choose Billing, and select Contact sales to begin the Enterprise conversation. Starter and Pro workspaces continue to sign in with standard Nimbus credentials.

chunks.heading: What changed from the 2025 pricing
chunks.text: If you have reviewed the previous pricing sheet, this section summarizes what is different. Three changes affect how plans compare, and each one is described below so you can see whether it touches your workspace. First, the Starter price rose from $8 to $9 per user per month compared with the 2025 pricing. Existing Starter customers will see the new rate reflected when their annual term renews. You can confirm your current rate by opening Settings, selecting Billing, and checking the Plan summary panel, which lists the per-user amount for your workspace. Second, two-factor authentication became available on the Free plan.

chunks.heading: What changed from the 2025 pricing
chunks.text: Previously, teams on Free had to upgrade to protect sign-ins with a second step. Now any Free workspace owner can go to Settings, choose Security, and turn on two-factor authentication for their account, then ask teammates to do the same. Third, the Enterprise API daily quota increased to 1,000,000 requests. This gives large organizations more headroom for integrations, scheduled jobs, and internal tooling that call the Nimbus API throughout the day. No action is needed to receive the higher quota; it applies automatically to Enterprise workspaces. All other plan details remain as described on the current sheet.

chunks.heading: Workspace roles and guest access
chunks.text: Every person in a Nimbus Platform workspace holds one of four roles: Owner, Admin, Member or Guest. The role decides what that person can see and change, so it is worth understanding each one before you start inviting people. The Owner is the person ultimately responsible for the workspace, including its plan and its settings. Admins help the Owner run the workspace. They manage people, security options and the administrative areas of the console. Members are the everyday users who create, edit and organize content. Guests are outside collaborators, such as contractors or clients, who need limited access to specific material.

chunks.heading: Workspace roles and guest access
chunks.text: Guests can view and comment on shared files, which makes them useful for review and feedback. They cannot create shared drives, so any space that an outside collaborator needs must be set up by a Member, Admin or Owner first, and the Guest is then given access to it. Guest access is available on Starter, Pro and Enterprise. Workspaces on the Free plan do not include it, so if you need to bring in external reviewers you will need to upgrade first. To change someone's role, open Settings, choose Members, find the person in the list and use the role menu beside their name. When in doubt, give people the lowest role that lets them do their work, and revisit the list regularly as teams change.

chunks.heading: Configuring single sign-on
chunks.text: Single sign-on lets people reach Nimbus Platform with the credentials they already use at work. Admins on Pro and Enterprise configure it under Settings > Security > Single sign-on. Begin by choosing the protocol your identity provider uses. For SAML 2.0, upload the identity provider metadata XML file that you export from your provider's application settings. For OIDC, enter the issuer URL and the client ID instead. Nimbus then shows you the values your provider needs in return, such as the callback address, so copy those back into the provider's configuration. Nimbus supports Okta, Microsoft Entra ID and Google Workspace as identity providers.

chunks.heading: Automated provisioning with SCIM
chunks.text: Enterprise admins can enable SCIM 2.0 provisioning so that the identity provider becomes the source of truth for who has an account. With SCIM in place, users can be created, updated and deactivated from the identity provider, and the changes appear in Nimbus without anyone editing the member list by hand. To set it up, open Settings > Security > Provisioning and generate a SCIM token. Copy it immediately and store it somewhere safe, because it works like a password for your provisioning connection. In your identity provider, add the Nimbus provisioning application, paste the token when prompted and enter the provisioning address shown in the Nimbus console.

chunks.heading: Automated provisioning with SCIM
chunks.text: Then run a test push with a single account to confirm that it arrives. SCIM tokens expire after 365 days. When a token expires, provisioning stops until you replace it, so it is wise to record the creation date and set a reminder well before the end of the period. To rotate a token, generate a new one under the same Provisioning screen, update the identity provider with the new value and confirm that a test change goes through. When someone leaves the company and is deactivated in the identity provider, their Nimbus account is deactivated too. Review the member list after your first synchronization to check that roles and names look as you expect.

chunks.heading: Audit logs and retention
chunks.text: Audit logs give admins a trustworthy record of what happened in the workspace. They record sign-ins, sharing changes, admin actions and file deletions. This makes them the first place to look when you need to answer questions such as who shared a folder externally, when a setting was changed or who removed an important file. Open the audit log from the admin console and use the filters to narrow events by person, event type or time range. Selecting an entry shows the details, including the actor and the item affected. Retention depends on your plan. Audit events are kept 1 year with the Pro add-on and 7 years on Enterprise.

chunks.heading: Audit logs and retention
chunks.text: Once events pass the retention window they are no longer available in the console, so if you have longer reporting obligations, export the data regularly rather than relying on the console alone. Audit logs can be exported as CSV. Choose a time range, select Export and download the file when it is ready. The CSV opens in any spreadsheet tool, which is convenient for ad hoc investigations and for sharing evidence with auditors. Enterprise can also export audit logs daily to an Amazon S3 bucket. This suits teams that feed events into a security monitoring system or keep records in their own storage. Configure the destination in the audit settings and check that the bucket permissions allow Nimbus to write to it.

chunks.heading: Two-factor authentication
chunks.text: Two-factor authentication adds a second check to sign-in, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account. Nimbus Platform supports three methods: an authenticator app (TOTP), SMS and passkeys. An authenticator app generates time-based codes on the user's phone and works without a mobile signal. Passkeys let people confirm their identity with a device biometric or security key, and they resist phishing better than typed codes. SMS sends a code by text message. SMS codes are being retired; see the release notes for the date. Encourage members to switch to an authenticator app or passkey now so they are not caught out when SMS stops.

chunks.heading: Two-factor authentication
chunks.text: Admins can require two-factor authentication for all members under Settings > Security > Two-factor. When you turn the requirement on, members who have not yet enrolled are prompted to set up a method the next time they sign in. They cannot continue into the workspace until enrollment is complete. Before you enforce the requirement, send a short message explaining what is changing and which methods you recommend. Include a link to the setup instructions and name a contact for people who lose their device. Afterward, check the member list for anyone who has not enrolled and follow up individually. Admins should enroll themselves first so they can help others.

chunks.heading: Shared drive limits
chunks.text: Shared drives give teams a common place for files that does not depend on any one person's account. Each workspace can hold a set number of shared drives, determined by its plan: Starter workspaces can have 50, Pro workspaces 500 and Enterprise workspaces 5,000. These allowances are generous for most organizations, but it helps to plan a structure before you create many drives. A common approach is to create one drive per team or per long-running project rather than one per document set. Give each drive a clear name, such as the department or client it serves, so members can find it in the sidebar without searching.

chunks.heading: Trash, retention and legal holds
chunks.text: When a file is deleted in Nimbus Platform it moves to the trash rather than disappearing immediately, which gives people time to recover mistakes. How long items stay depends on the plan: Free keeps deleted files for 14 days, Starter for 30 days, Pro for 60 days and Enterprise for 90 days. After that period, files are permanently deleted and cannot be restored. To recover a file, open the trash, select the item and choose Restore. It returns to its original location if that location still exists. Otherwise it appears in the top level of the owner's files. Only Owners and Admins can empty the trash.

chunks.heading: Trash, retention and legal holds
chunks.text: Members can delete their own files but cannot purge them early, which protects the workspace against accidental or careless permanent removal. If you do need to clear the trash, review the contents first, since emptying it cannot be undone. Enterprise workspaces also have legal holds. A legal hold prevents permanent deletion of the held files until the hold is released, even after the trash period has passed. This is useful when the organization must preserve material for an investigation or legal matter. Apply holds only to what is necessary, and record who authorized each hold. When the matter closes, release the hold so normal retention can resume for those files.

chunks.heading: Data residency
chunks.text: Data residency determines the geographic region where your workspace content is stored. Enterprise workspaces can choose the US, EU (Frankfurt) or APAC (Tokyo) region when the workspace is created. Pick the one that best matches your regulatory obligations, your customers' expectations and where most of your people work. Make this decision carefully, because the region cannot be changed later. If your needs change, moving regions requires a migration by support. That means opening a support request, agreeing a plan with the support team and coordinating a time that causes the least disruption to your teams. It is far easier to choose correctly at the start than to migrate afterward.

This walkthrough covers the essentials of setting up a new workspace: bringing in your people and creating a shared drive for them to work in. Start by signing in with your admin account and opening the admin console from the account menu. Spend a few minutes looking at the sidebar so you know where members, security settings and drives are located. To invite members:
1. Open Settings and choose Members. 2. Select Invite people. 3. Enter email addresses, separated by commas or on new lines. 4. Choose a role for the group. Member is the right choice for most colleagues. 5. Add an optional personal note, then send the invitations.

chunks.heading: Managing members
chunks.text: Over time people change teams, take leave or leave the company, and admins need to keep the member list accurate. Nimbus Platform lets you deactivate, reactivate and hand over files without losing work. To deactivate a member, open Settings, choose Members and locate the person. Open the menu beside their name and select Deactivate. The person can no longer sign in, but their account and content are preserved so nothing disappears unexpectedly. Deactivation is the right choice when someone leaves, because it removes access immediately while you decide what to do with their files.

To reactivate, find the deactivated person in the member list, using the status filter if needed, and select Reactivate. They regain access with the role they previously held, though it is worth confirming that the role is still appropriate. Before or after deactivating someone, transfer ownership of their files so that colleagues can keep working on them:
1. Open the person's entry in the member list. 2. Choose Transfer files. 3. Select the colleague who should become the new owner. 4. Review the summary and confirm. Choose a recipient who actually understands the content, ideally the person's manager or successor. After the transfer, let the new owner know so they can check sharing settings and tidy anything that is no longer relevant.

chunks.text: Sharing in Nimbus Platform is designed to be quick, while keeping you in control of who can see your work. You can share a file with people in your workspace, with guests outside your organization, or by link. Choose whichever fits the situation: teammates are usually the simplest choice, guests suit contractors and clients, and links work well when you want to post a file in a message or document. Put the request at the start of the message, for example asking a colleague to confirm a figure, and mention only the people who need to act. chunks.text: Version history is your safety net when a file changes in a way you did not intend. Whether a colleague overwrote a paragraph or you saved over the wrong draft, you can go back to an earlier version of the file and restore it. To restore a version, find the file in your file list or open it, then open the file's menu and choose Version history. A panel lists the saved versions of that file, usually with the time of each save and the name of the person who made the change. Select an entry to preview it.

The earlier version becomes the current file, and your work is not lost, because the version you replaced stays available in the list. Workspace admins can confirm the details for their plan and decide whether a different one would suit the team better. It helps to check version history before making large edits to an important file. If something goes wrong, you will know exactly where to go to recover it.

chunks.heading: Searching for files
chunks.text: Search is the fastest way to find your work in Nimbus Platform once your workspace grows. The search box sits at the top of every screen. Start typing and results appear as you go, so you can often jump straight to a file without pressing Enter. Search looks at file names and also at the text inside documents, PDFs and slides. That means you do not need to remember what a file was called. If you recall a phrase from a contract, a heading in a presentation, or a line from meeting notes, type it and the matching files are listed.

Files you did not prepare may not open, and features that rely on the network, such as sharing, mentions and search across the workspace, will wait until you reconnect. Once you are back online, the app syncs your changes automatically. Give it a moment to finish before closing the browser tab.

To see the full list for your device, open the help menu in the web app and choose Keyboard shortcuts. A panel appears showing each action beside its key combination. The keys differ slightly by system: on Windows and Linux the main modifier is usually Ctrl, while on a Mac it is Command. The panel shows the right keys for the computer you are using. chunks.heading: Installing Nimbus Sync
chunks.text: Nimbus Sync keeps a folder on your computer in step with your Nimbus workspace, so files you save locally appear online and changes made by teammates arrive on your device. Before you begin, confirm that your computer meets the system requirements. Nimbus Sync 5.x runs on Windows 10 or later, macOS 13 or later, and Ubuntu 22.04 or later. If your team uses Ubuntu 24.04, packages for that release are available starting with Nimbus Sync 5.3, so make sure you choose a build at or beyond that release. To install, sign in to the Nimbus web app in your browser. Open the Help menu and choose Download Sync.

briefs: Pausing and resuming sync, and reading the status icons
Resolving sync conflicts and conflicted copies
chunks.heading: Installing Nimbus Sync
chunks.text: The web app detects your operating system and offers the matching installer, though you can pick a different one from the list if you are preparing a different machine. Step 1: Run the downloaded installer and accept the license terms. Step 2: Follow the prompts and let the installer finish. On macOS, drag the app into Applications when asked. Step 3: Launch Nimbus Sync and sign in with your Nimbus account. Enterprise users with single sign-on will be redirected to their identity provider. Step 4: Choose the location of your Nimbus folder and confirm.

chunks.heading: Installing Nimbus Sync
chunks.text: After sign-in, the app appears in the system tray or menu bar, and your first sync begins automatically. Keep the window open until the status icon settles, which indicates your files are ready to use.

chunks.heading: Choosing folders with selective sync
chunks.text: Not every device needs every file. Selective sync lets you choose which folders are stored on the device, while all other folders remain online-only. This is especially useful on laptops with limited storage, or when you belong to a workspace with large shared archives that you rarely touch. To set it up, open the Nimbus Sync menu from the system tray or menu bar and select Preferences. Switch to the Sync tab and click Choose folders. A tree of your workspace appears with a checkbox beside each folder. Tick the folders you want kept on this computer and clear the ones you do not.

Resolving sync conflicts and conflicted copies
chunks.heading: Choosing folders with selective sync
chunks.text: When you click Apply, Nimbus Sync downloads newly selected folders and removes the local copies of any you cleared. Nothing is deleted from your workspace; the files stay safely online and can be reached from the web app at any time. Online-only items still show up in your Nimbus folder in File Explorer or Finder, marked with a small cloud badge. Online-only files download when opened, so double-clicking one fetches it and then launches it in the associated application. Once downloaded, it behaves like any other local file and syncs changes back as you save. You can change your selection whenever your needs shift. Each device keeps its own choices, so a work desktop and a personal laptop can hold different sets of folders.

chunks.heading: File size, names, and path limits
chunks.text: Nimbus Sync enforces a few rules so that files behave consistently across Windows, macOS, and Linux. Knowing them ahead of time helps you avoid files that refuse to upload. File size: the maximum file size is 15 GB on Free and Starter, and 250 GB on Pro and Enterprise. If a file is larger than your plan allows, Nimbus Sync skips it and shows a warning in the activity list. Consider splitting or compressing the file, or ask your administrator about moving to a plan with a higher allowance. Names: file and folder names cannot contain the characters < > : " / \ | ? *.

briefs: Pausing and resuming sync, and reading the status icons
Resolving sync conflicts and conflicted copies
chunks.heading: File size, names, and path limits
chunks.text: These characters are reserved by at least one supported operating system, so allowing them could make a file unreadable elsewhere. If you try to save an item with one of them in its name, the app will flag it. Rename the item by removing or replacing the character, for example using a hyphen in place of a colon in a dated report title. Path length: the full path of a synced file cannot exceed 400 characters. The path includes your Nimbus folder location and every parent folder name, so deeply nested structures with long descriptive names can reach the limit sooner than expected. If a file is skipped for this reason, shorten a folder name higher up the tree or move the file closer to the top of your workspace.

briefs: Pausing and resuming sync, and reading the status icons
Resolving sync conflicts and conflicted copies
chunks.heading: Managing bandwidth and metered connections
chunks.text: Sync can compete with video calls and downloads for your network, so Nimbus Sync gives you control over how much it uses. Upload and download limits can be set under Preferences > Network. Open the Nimbus Sync menu in the system tray or menu bar, choose Preferences, and select the Network tab. In the Bandwidth section you will see separate controls for download and upload. By default, both are unrestricted. To cap either one, change the setting from Don't limit to Limit to, then enter a rate in the field provided. Click Apply and the new limit takes effect immediately, without restarting the app.

briefs: Pausing and resuming sync, and reading the status icons
Resolving sync conflicts and conflicted copies
chunks.heading: Managing bandwidth and metered connections
chunks.text: Many people leave downloads unrestricted and cap uploads, since large uploads are the most likely to saturate a home connection and slow a call. Nimbus Sync also looks after your data allowance. Sync pauses automatically on metered connections unless the user turns this off. This applies to connections your operating system identifies as metered, such as a mobile hotspot or a capped data plan. While paused, the status icon shows that sync is waiting, and it resumes once you join a standard network. If you would rather keep syncing on a metered connection, clear the option labeled Pause on metered networks in the same Network tab. Consider keeping it enabled when travelling, so large files do not use up your data unexpectedly.

briefs: Pausing and resuming sync, and reading the status icons
Resolving sync conflicts and conflicted copies
chunks.heading: Pausing, resuming, and reading status icons
chunks.text: Sometimes you want Nimbus Sync to stand still, perhaps while you are presenting, working on a slow connection, or making a large batch of edits you are not ready to share. You can pause sync at any time without signing out or closing the app. To pause, click the Nimbus Sync icon in the system tray on Windows and Linux, or the menu bar on macOS. Choose Pause syncing from the menu. Changes you make while paused are remembered locally and are not lost. To continue, open the same menu and choose Resume syncing. The app then uploads your pending changes and downloads anything new from your workspace.

Resolving sync conflicts and conflicted copies
chunks.heading: Pausing, resuming, and reading status icons
chunks.text:
The status icon tells you what the app is doing at a glance:

- A steady cloud with a check mark means everything is up to date.
- Circling arrows mean files are currently being uploaded or downloaded.
- Two parallel bars mean sync is paused, either by you or automatically.
- A warning triangle means some items need attention, such as a name problem or a conflicted copy.
- A gray cloud with a slash means the app cannot reach Nimbus, usually because the device is offline or you have been signed out.

briefs: Pausing and resuming sync, and reading the status icons
Resolving sync conflicts and conflicted copies
chunks.heading: Pausing, resuming, and reading status icons
chunks.text: Hover over the icon to see a short summary, or click it to open the activity list with details for each affected file. If the icon stays on the arrows for a long time, check your network connection, then try pausing and resuming to nudge the app into scanning again.

Resolving sync conflicts and conflicted copies
chunks.heading: Resolving sync conflicts
chunks.text: A sync conflict happens when the same file is changed in different places before those changes have had a chance to reach each other. A common example is editing a document on a laptop while offline, while a colleague updates the same document in the web app. When the laptop reconnects, Nimbus Sync cannot safely decide which edit should win, so it keeps both versions rather than overwriting either. The version that was already in your workspace keeps its original name. Your local edit is saved beside it as a conflicted copy, with your device name and a date added to the file name.

briefs: Pausing and resuming sync, and reading the status icons
Resolving sync conflicts and conflicted copies
chunks.heading: Resolving sync conflicts
chunks.text:
The status icon shows a warning triangle, and the activity list names the affected file. To resolve it, follow these steps:

Step 1: Open both files side by side. Use the Show in folder option in the activity list to find them quickly. Step 2: Compare the content and decide what should be kept. For text documents, copy the changes you want from one file into the other. Step 3: Save the final version under the original file name. Step 4: Delete the conflicted copy once you are satisfied. After the extra file is removed, the warning clears on the next sync.

briefs: Pausing and resuming sync, and reading the status icons
Resolving sync conflicts and conflicted copies
chunks.heading: Resolving sync conflicts
chunks.text: To avoid repeat conflicts, let sync finish before closing your laptop, and agree with teammates about who edits shared files at a given time. Previous versions can also be restored from the web app if you need to go back.

Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Error code reference: local and account errors
chunks.text: When Nimbus Sync cannot complete an operation, it shows an error code in the status panel of the desktop client and records the same code in the sync log. Knowing what each code means is the quickest way to decide whether you can fix the problem yourself or need to involve an administrator. This section covers the codes that most often relate to the local machine, file naming, and account status. E1001 means the local disk is full. The client has nowhere to write the files it is trying to download, so syncing pauses until space is available.

briefs: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Error code reference: local and account errors
chunks.text: Free up space by emptying the recycle bin, removing large files you no longer need, or choosing selective sync so that fewer folders are stored on the device. Once space is available, the client resumes automatically. E2207 means a file name contains characters the server does not allow. The file stays on your computer but is skipped during upload, and it appears in the activity list with a warning icon. Other files continue to sync normally. E4013 means the account was suspended, either by an admin or for non-payment. While an account is suspended, the client stops syncing and prompts you to sign in again. Individual users cannot clear this state themselves. Contact your workspace administrator, who can review the account status and billing details in the admin console.

briefs: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Error code reference: authentication, devices and server
chunks.text: The remaining common codes relate to sign-in sessions, device registration, and the availability of the Nimbus service. They usually appear as a banner at the top of the client window and as a red badge on the tray or menu bar icon. E4012 means the client failed to refresh its OAuth access token. This usually happens because the refresh token was revoked, for example after a password reset or an administrator ending your sessions, or because the device clock is more than 5 minutes off from the correct time. Tokens are time sensitive, so even a healthy session can be rejected when the local clock drifts.

briefs: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Error code reference: authentication, devices and server
chunks.text: E4019 means the user has reached the device limit for the plan. Each computer or mobile device that signs in to Nimbus Sync counts toward that limit, and a new sign-in is refused until a slot is available. The error is tied to your user account rather than to the specific machine you are using at the moment. E5003 means the server is temporarily unavailable. This is not a problem with your device or account. The client retries with backoff, meaning it waits progressively longer between attempts so it does not add load while the service recovers. You do not need to restart the client, and pending changes are kept until the connection succeeds.

briefs: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Fixing E4012 token refresh failures
chunks.text: If the client reports E4012, it could not renew its OAuth access token and has stopped syncing until the session is restored. Work through the following steps in order, checking the client status after each one. 1) Set the device clock to update automatically. Open the date and time settings of your operating system and turn on the option to set the time and time zone automatically. A clock that has drifted is a frequent cause of E4012, and correcting it often clears the error without any further action. 2) Sign out of Nimbus Sync and sign in again.

briefs: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Fixing E4012 token refresh failures
chunks.text: Use the account menu in the client, choose the sign-out option, then sign in with your usual credentials. This replaces the stored tokens with a fresh set. 3) If the workspace uses SSO, sign in to the identity provider in a browser to renew the session. Once your identity provider session is active again, return to the client and try signing in. 4) If the error continues, contact support with the sync log. Support can see why the token was rejected much faster when the log is attached. To create the file, export the sync log under Help > Export logs. Choose a location you can easily find, such as the desktop, and attach the exported file to your support request along with a short description of what you already tried.

briefs: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Fixing E4019 and E2207
chunks.text: Two of the most common problems that users can resolve themselves are device limit errors and file name errors. Both have straightforward fixes. To fix E4019, remove an old device under Settings > Devices in the web app. Sign in to Nimbus from a browser, open your account settings, and select the Devices tab. You will see a list of every computer and phone that has signed in, along with its name and the time it was last active. Look for machines you no longer use, such as a replaced laptop or a test virtual machine, and choose the remove option next to each one.

briefs: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Fixing E4019 and E2207
chunks.text: After a device is removed, return to the client that showed the error and sign in again. If every listed device is still in use, the alternative is to upgrade the plan, since the device limit depends on your plan. Ask your workspace administrator if plan changes are managed centrally. To fix E2207, rename the file to remove the reserved characters. Find the file in the activity list, where the warning icon identifies it, and open its location on your computer. Change the name so it uses only letters, digits, spaces, hyphens, and underscores. Avoid copying names from other systems that permit symbols the Nimbus server rejects. After renaming, the client picks up the change and uploads the file on its next pass.

briefs: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
chunks.text: A well prepared support request is resolved much faster than a vague one. Before you get in touch, spend a few minutes gathering the information that the support team will almost certainly ask for. Doing this up front avoids repeated back-and-forth messages. Start by noting exactly what you were doing when the problem appeared. Write down the name of the file or folder involved, whether the problem affects a single device or all of them, and whether it began after a change such as an operating system update, a new network, or a password reset.

briefs: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
chunks.text: If the client displayed an error code or message, copy it exactly as shown or take a screenshot of the status panel. Next, confirm the basics. Check that you can reach the Nimbus web app in a browser, that your internet connection is stable, and that you are signed in to the expected account. Make a note of your operating system and the client version, which you can find in the About section of the Help menu. Finally, export the sync log from the Help menu and save it somewhere easy to find. Reproduce the problem once more if you can, then export the log right afterward so it contains the relevant events. Attach the log, your notes, and any screenshots to the support request.

briefs: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.text: Security software protects your computer, but it can sometimes interfere with Nimbus Sync. Typical symptoms include files that stay stuck in a pending state, uploads that never finish, repeated connection warnings, or a client that cannot sign in even though the web app works normally in your browser. Begin by checking whether your antivirus program has quarantined or blocked any Nimbus files. Open its protection history or event log and look for entries that mention Nimbus Sync or files inside your sync folder. If something was flagged incorrectly, restore it and add an exclusion for the Nimbus Sync application and for the sync folder itself.

briefs: Collecting diagnostics before contacting support
Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.heading: Problems with antivirus and firewall software
chunks.text: Excluding the folder stops real-time scanning from locking files while the client is trying to read or update them. Next, review your firewall. The client needs outbound access to the internet over secure connections. In your firewall settings, make sure the Nimbus Sync program is on the list of allowed applications for both private and public networks. On managed company computers, ask your IT team to allow the client, because local changes may be overridden by central policy. After changing any setting, restart the client and watch the status panel to see whether syncing resumes. If it does not, temporarily pause the security software only long enough to test, then turn it back on and share your findings with support.

chunks.heading: Authentication overview
chunks.text: Nimbus Gateway authenticates every request that reaches your workspace, and you can choose between two methods depending on how your integration runs. API keys are the simplest option and suit scripts, internal tools and server-side jobs where a single trusted service calls the Gateway. OAuth 2.0 client credentials suit integrations that need a short-lived access token, for example a backend service that you want to manage through your identity provider instead of storing a long-lived secret. To create a key, sign in as a workspace admin and open Settings > Developer > API keys.

chunks.heading: Authentication overview
chunks.text: Select Create key, give it a descriptive name such as the service or environment that will use it, and choose the access it should carry. The full key value is displayed only at creation time, so copy it straight into your secrets manager. If you lose it, delete the key and generate a replacement. API keys expire after 1 year, and the console shows the expiry date next to each entry. Do not wait for expiry to replace them. We recommend rotating keys every 90 days: create the new key, deploy it to your services, confirm traffic is flowing with it, and only then revoke the old key. Using separate keys for staging and production makes this routine much safer, and it lets you revoke a single compromised key without interrupting unrelated integrations.

chunks.heading: Quotas and rate limits
chunks.text: Every workspace on Nimbus Gateway is subject to two kinds of limits: a daily API quota and a per-second burst limit. The daily quota caps the total volume of calls your workspace can make in a day, while the burst limit controls how many calls can arrive in a short moment. Both values depend on your plan, so the numbers for Starter, Pro and Enterprise differ. Consult the pricing sheet for the figures that apply to you rather than hard-coding assumptions into your client. When a request goes over either limit, the Gateway rejects it with HTTP 429 and the error code E4290.

chunks.heading: Quotas and rate limits
chunks.text: The response also includes a Retry-After header that states how many seconds to wait before sending the request again. Your client should read that header and pause for the stated time instead of retrying immediately, since an instant retry will almost certainly fail and can prolong the problem. A few habits keep you well inside your limits. Spread scheduled jobs out instead of starting them all at the same moment. Cache responses that rarely change. Queue bulk operations and release them at a steady pace.

chunks.text: If you see E4290 frequently even after smoothing your traffic, review the usage view in the console to see whether the daily quota or the burst limit is the one being reached, then consider whether a different plan fits your workload.

chunks.heading: Receiving webhooks
chunks.text: Nimbus Gateway can notify your systems by sending webhooks to an HTTPS endpoint that you register in the developer settings. Because anyone who discovers your endpoint address could post data to it, you should always verify that a delivery genuinely came from the Gateway before acting on it. Each webhook is signed with an HMAC-SHA256 signature, which is placed in the X-Nimbus-Signature header. To verify a delivery, read the raw request body exactly as it arrived, compute an HMAC-SHA256 digest of that body using your webhook signing secret, and compare the result with the header value. Use a constant-time comparison function so that timing differences reveal nothing.

briefs: Making the first API call with curl

Testing webhooks locally
chunks.heading: Receiving webhooks
chunks.text: If the values do not match, reject the request and do not process the payload. A common mistake is parsing the JSON and re-serializing it before computing the digest; this changes whitespace and key order and causes valid signatures to fail. Your endpoint should acknowledge a delivery quickly with a success status and do heavy work afterward in a background job. If your endpoint is unavailable or returns an error, the Gateway treats the delivery as failed. Failed deliveries are retried 5 times with exponential backoff over 24 hours, and after that the event is dropped. Make your handler safe to run more than once for the same event, because retries can result in duplicates, and monitor your endpoint so that events are not lost.

chunks.heading: Regional endpoints
chunks.text: Nimbus Gateway is served from regional endpoints so that your traffic can stay close to your users and your stored data. The available hosts are api.us.nimbus.example, api.eu.nimbus.example and api.apac.nimbus.example. Choose the host that matches the region where your workspace operates, and keep that value in configuration instead of scattering it through your code, which makes later changes straightforward. For Enterprise workspaces the choice is not optional. An Enterprise workspace must call the endpoint of its data residency region. If your data is held in the European region, for example, your integrations must send requests to api.eu.nimbus.example.

chunks.heading: Regional endpoints
chunks.text: Calling a different regional host is not supported for these workspaces and may be rejected. You can confirm your workspace's residency region in the workspace settings of the console before you configure your clients. Other plans also benefit from picking the nearest region, mainly because shorter network paths usually mean lower latency for your callers. Whichever host you use, authentication works the same way, and the credentials you created for your workspace are presented in the same manner. When you deploy across several environments, make the base URL an environment variable, and add a startup check that logs which regional host each service is using. This makes misconfigurations easy to spot during rollout and during incident reviews.

chunks.heading: Making the first API call with curl
chunks.text: The quickest way to confirm that your credentials work is to send a request from the command line with curl. Before you begin, make sure you have created an API key in the developer settings and that you know the regional host for your workspace. Store the key in an environment variable rather than typing it directly into your shell history. First, export your key, for example by setting a variable named NIMBUS_API_KEY in your terminal session. Next, build the request. Use the GET method against a simple read-only path on your regional host, and include an Authorization header that carries your key as a bearer token.

chunks.heading: Making the first API call with curl
chunks.text: Also add an Accept header asking for JSON so the response is easy to read. Add the silent-with-errors and include-headers options if you want to see status information alongside the body. After you run the command, check the status line. A success status means the Gateway accepted your credentials and returned data. An unauthorized status usually means the key was copied incorrectly, was revoked, or has expired. A forbidden status suggests the key lacks the access needed for that path. If the command hangs or cannot resolve the host, double-check the hostname spelling and your network or proxy settings. When the call works, pipe the output through a JSON formatter to explore the structure, then move the same request into your application code.

chunks.heading: Idempotency keys and safe retries
chunks.text: Networks fail in awkward ways. A client may send a request that the Gateway processes successfully, yet never receive the response because the connection drops. If the client simply sends the request again, the operation could be performed twice. Idempotency keys exist to prevent that outcome by letting you mark a request as a repeat of an earlier attempt. The approach is straightforward. Before sending an operation that creates or changes something, generate a unique value, such as a random identifier, and send it in an Idempotency-Key header. Save that value alongside the pending operation in your own storage.

briefs: Making the first API call with curl

Testing webhooks locally
chunks.heading: Idempotency keys and safe retries
chunks.text: If you must retry, reuse the exact same value and the same request body. The service can then recognize the repeat and return the original outcome instead of repeating the work. Never reuse a key for a different operation, and generate a fresh value whenever the intent of the request changes. Pair idempotency keys with a sensible retry policy. Retry only when the failure is likely temporary, such as a timeout, a connection error or a server-side error. Do not retry requests that failed because of invalid input, since the result will not change. When the Gateway tells you to slow down, honor the wait time it provides. Add a growing delay with a little random jitter between attempts, and set a sensible cap on the total number of attempts so that failures eventually surface to your monitoring.

chunks.heading: Testing webhooks locally
chunks.text: Developing a webhook handler is easier when you can receive real deliveries on your own machine. Because the Gateway sends events over the public internet, your laptop needs a reachable address. The usual solution is a tunneling tool that gives you a temporary public HTTPS URL and forwards incoming traffic to a port on your computer. Start your handler locally and confirm it responds on its port. Then launch your tunneling tool and copy the public URL it prints. Open the developer settings in the console, add a new webhook endpoint, and paste that URL along with the path your handler listens on.

chunks.heading: Testing webhooks locally
chunks.text: Save the endpoint and note the signing secret displayed for it, then place the secret in your local environment configuration. Now trigger an event by performing an action in a test workspace, or use the test delivery option if your console offers it. Watch your handler's logs to confirm that the request arrived. Verify the signature from the request header against the raw body, exactly as you will in production, so that mistakes surface early. Many developers also save sample payloads to disk, which lets them replay events with curl without repeating the original action. When you finish, remove the temporary endpoint from the console and shut down the tunnel. Replace it with your permanent staging address so that stale tunnel URLs do not keep receiving events or generating failed deliveries.

chunks.heading: Dashboards, widgets and refresh rates
chunks.text: Dashboards are the main workspace in Nimbus Analytics. Each dashboard is a canvas of widgets, and every widget displays the result of a saved query as a chart, table, single-value tile or text note. You can drag widgets to reposition them, resize them from the corner handle, and group related widgets under a shared heading so that viewers can scan the page quickly. The number of widgets you can place on a single dashboard depends on your plan. Starter dashboards can hold 10 widgets, Pro dashboards can hold 40 widgets, and Enterprise dashboards can hold 200 widgets.

briefs: Building a first dashboard from a data source
Sharing dashboards and controlling who can edit them
chunks.heading: Dashboards, widgets and refresh rates
chunks.text: When a dashboard reaches its limit, the Add Widget button is disabled and a banner explains why. To make room, remove widgets you no longer need or split the content into a second dashboard organized around a different audience or topic. Dashboards also refresh at different rates depending on the plan. On Starter, dashboards refresh hourly. On Pro, they refresh every 15 minutes, and on Enterprise they refresh every minute, which suits operational views that teams keep open on a wall display. A small timestamp in the top-right corner of each dashboard shows when the data was last updated. If you need to see the newest figures sooner than the next scheduled refresh, open the dashboard menu and choose Refresh Now to rerun the underlying queries immediately.

chunks.heading: Connecting data sources
chunks.text: Before you can build charts, Nimbus Analytics needs a connection to the place where your data lives. Administrators manage these connections from Settings, under Data Sources. The supported connectors are PostgreSQL, Snowflake, BigQuery and Amazon S3, which together cover most transactional databases, cloud warehouses and file-based data lakes. To add a connector, select Add Data Source and pick the connector type from the gallery. The form that follows asks for the details that connector needs. For PostgreSQL this is typically the host, port, database name and credentials. For Snowflake and BigQuery you will provide account or project information along with a service identity.

briefs: Building a first dashboard from a data source
Sharing dashboards and controlling who can edit them
chunks.heading: Connecting data sources
chunks.text: For Amazon S3 you specify the bucket, the folder path that holds your files, and access credentials with read permission. We recommend creating a dedicated read-only account for Nimbus Analytics so that it can never modify your source data. Select Test Connection before saving. A green confirmation means Nimbus Analytics can reach the source and read its schema. Enterprise customers who need to reach a system outside this list can also add custom JDBC connectors. This option appears in the connector gallery as Custom JDBC, and it asks for a driver, a connection string and credentials. Once a source is saved, it becomes available to everyone who has permission to write queries in your workspace.

briefs: Building a first dashboard from a data source
Sharing dashboards and controlling who can edit them
chunks.heading: Scheduled reports and delivery
chunks.text: Scheduled reports let you deliver the contents of a dashboard to people who do not log in to Nimbus Analytics every day. Open any dashboard, choose Schedule from the toolbar, and the schedule panel will appear on the right. Here you set how often the report runs, the time of day, the time zone, and the recipients. Reports are sent by email, and you can choose whether each message carries a PDF or a CSV attachment. PDF works well for executives and anyone who wants to see charts laid out as they appear on screen.

briefs: Building a first dashboard from a data source
Sharing dashboards and controlling who can edit them
chunks.heading: Scheduled reports and delivery
chunks.text: CSV is better for analysts who plan to open the figures in a spreadsheet or pass them into another tool. You can add a short message to the email body to explain what the recipient is looking at and who to contact with questions. The number of schedules available depends on your plan. Pro workspaces can have up to 20 report schedules, so it is worth combining recipients who need the same content into a single schedule rather than creating duplicates. Enterprise workspaces have no limit on report schedules. You can pause a schedule at any time from the Schedules list, and you can review or delete schedules that are no longer useful so your team stays organized.

chunks.heading: Query history
chunks.text: Every time someone runs a query in Nimbus Analytics, whether from the query editor or through a widget that executes a saved query, the run is recorded in Query History. You can open it from the left navigation. It is a handy way to recover a query you wrote earlier, check what a colleague ran against a data source, or investigate why a chart suddenly shows different numbers. Query history is kept for 90 days. After that period, older entries are removed automatically and can no longer be viewed or restored. If a query is important to your team, do not rely on history alone to preserve it.

briefs: Building a first dashboard from a data source
Sharing dashboards and controlling who can edit them
chunks.heading: Query history
chunks.text: Open the entry and choose Save Query, give it a clear name, and add a short description so that others can find and reuse it. The history list shows the query text, the data source it ran against, the person who ran it, and the time it started. Use the filter bar above the list to narrow results by data source, user or keyword. Selecting an entry opens a detail view where you can copy the text, reopen it in the editor, or see whether the run completed or failed. When you reopen a query, the editor loads it as a new draft, so the original history entry stays unchanged.

Sharing dashboards and controlling who can edit them
chunks.heading: Building your first dashboard
chunks.text: This walkthrough takes you from a connected data source to a working dashboard. Make sure an administrator has already added a source under Settings, then follow these steps. Step 1. Select Dashboards in the left navigation and choose New Dashboard. Give it a descriptive name, such as Weekly Sales Overview, and an optional description so others understand its purpose. Step 2. Select Add Widget. Nimbus Analytics asks you to choose a data source. Pick the one that holds the information you want to show. Step 3. Write or select a query.

briefs: Building a first dashboard from a data source
Sharing dashboards and controlling who can edit them
chunks.heading: Building your first dashboard
chunks.text: If you are new to the query editor, start with a simple statement that returns a few columns, then choose Run to preview the results in a table below the editor. Adjust the query until the rows look right. Step 4. Pick a visualization. Line charts suit trends over time, bar charts suit comparisons between categories, and single-value tiles suit headline figures. Use the settings panel to assign columns to axes, rename labels and choose colors. Step 5. Save the widget and arrange it on the canvas. Drag it into position and resize it to fit with its neighbors. Repeat for additional widgets, grouping related ones together. Step 6. Review the layout in preview mode, then select Save. Your dashboard is ready to share with colleagues.

chunks.heading: Sharing dashboards and editing permissions
chunks.text: Once a dashboard is ready, you can share it with colleagues and decide exactly what each person is allowed to do. Open the dashboard and select Share in the upper-right corner. The sharing panel lists everyone who currently has access and the role each person holds. To invite someone, type a name or email address into the field at the top of the panel. Choose a role from the dropdown beside it. The Viewer role lets a person open the dashboard, change filters and export what they see, but they cannot alter the layout or the queries behind it.

briefs: Building a first dashboard from a data source
Sharing dashboards and controlling who can edit them
chunks.heading: Sharing dashboards and editing permissions
chunks.text: The Editor role lets a person add, move and remove widgets and change the queries that power them. Reserve Editor access for people who understand the data and are responsible for keeping the dashboard accurate. You can also share with a whole team at once by entering a team name, which is easier to maintain than adding individuals as people join and leave. If someone changes responsibilities, return to the sharing panel and update their role or remove them entirely. As a good habit, keep a small group of editors and make everyone else a viewer. Review the list occasionally, especially for dashboards that contain sensitive figures, and remove access that is no longer needed. Changes to roles take effect as soon as you save.

chunks.heading: Getting started with the Gateway API
chunks.text: The Nimbus Gateway REST API gives you programmatic access to the same content and administration features you use in the Nimbus console. It is available on the Starter, Pro and Enterprise plans. This reference describes how to make your first request and what to expect in return. The base URL for workspaces hosted in the United States is https://api.us.nimbus.example/v2. If your workspace is hosted in Europe or Asia Pacific, use the regional host for EU or APAC instead of the US host. The path after the host stays the same, so code written against one region works against another once you change the base URL.

briefs: Files resource: upload, download and metadata fields
Users resource: invite, update and deactivate
chunks.doc_title: Nimbus Gateway REST API v2 reference
chunks.heading: Getting started with the Gateway API
chunks.text:
You can confirm your workspace region in the console under your workspace settings. All requests use HTTPS and JSON. Send request bodies as JSON, set the Content-Type header to application/json, and expect JSON in every response. Authenticate each call with the Authorization header. Create a key in the console, copy it when it is shown, and store it somewhere secure, because you will not be able to view it again. A minimal request looks like this:

curl https://api.us.nimbus.example/v2/files \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"

If the call succeeds, you receive a JSON document describing the items you are allowed to see.

chunks.heading: Getting started with the Gateway API
chunks.text: If the header is missing or the credential is not accepted, the API returns an error object that explains what went wrong. Treat your credentials like a password and never embed them in client-side code.

chunks.doc_title: Nimbus Gateway REST API v2 reference
chunks.heading: Resources and pagination
chunks.text: The Gateway API is organized around a small set of resources, each addressed by its own path beneath the base URL. You will work with /files and /folders to manage content and its hierarchy, /users to manage the people in your workspace, /shared-drives to manage team spaces, and /webhooks to register endpoints that receive notifications when something changes. Each resource follows the same conventions, so once you are comfortable with one, the others feel familiar. Collections are returned by list endpoints, for example a GET request to /folders or /users. Rather than returning everything at once, list endpoints are paginated with a cursor.

briefs: Files resource: upload, download and metadata fields
Users resource: invite, update and deactivate
chunks.doc_title: Nimbus Gateway REST API v2 reference
chunks.heading: Resources and pagination
chunks.text: The response contains an array of items along with a cursor value that marks where the next page begins. To continue, send the same request again and include that cursor as a query parameter. When a response arrives without a cursor, you have reached the end of the collection. The default page size is 50 items. If you need fewer or more results per request, pass a limit parameter, up to a maximum page size of 200 items. Requests that ask for more than the maximum are not expanded beyond it, so write your loops to follow the cursor instead of assuming a single response is complete. A good practice is to keep filters and sort options identical while you walk through pages, and to treat cursors as opaque strings that you pass back unchanged.

chunks.doc_title: Nimbus Gateway REST API v2 reference
chunks.heading: Error codes and troubleshooting
chunks.text: When a request fails, the Gateway API returns a JSON error object containing a code, a short message and, where useful, a hint about how to fix the problem. Use the code, not the message text, to decide how your application should react. Client-side errors begin with E4. E4001 means the request was a bad request, usually because a field is missing or malformed, so check your JSON body and query parameters. E4010 means the API key is invalid, which often points to a copy and paste mistake. E4011 means the API key has expired, and you should create a replacement key in the console and update your configuration.

briefs: Files resource: upload, download and metadata fields
Users resource: invite, update and deactivate
chunks.doc_title: Nimbus Gateway REST API v2 reference
chunks.heading: Error codes and troubleshooting
chunks.text: E4012 means the OAuth token has expired or been revoked; refresh the token, or send the user back through the authorization flow if refreshing fails. E4290 means you exceeded the rate limit. Slow down, and wait before sending the request again, ideally with a gradually increasing delay between attempts. Server-side errors begin with E5. E5003 indicates an upstream service is unavailable. This is normally temporary, so retry after a pause and check the Nimbus status page if it persists. E5040 means the request timed out after 30 seconds. For long operations, narrow the scope of the call, for example by requesting fewer items, and try again. Log the full error object whenever you contact support, as it speeds up diagnosis.

chunks.doc_title: Nimbus Gateway REST API v2 reference
chunks.heading: Deprecation of the earlier API
chunks.text: If your integration still calls the earlier generation of the Nimbus Gateway API, you should plan a migration now. API v1 is deprecated and will be shut down on June 30, 2027. After that date, requests sent to the old endpoints will no longer be served, and any automation that depends on them will stop working. You do not have to wait to find out whether you are affected. Every v1 request returns a Deprecation header in its response. You can check for it in your logs, in your HTTP client's debugging output, or by running a single request with the verbose flag in curl.

briefs: Files resource: upload, download and metadata fields
Users resource: invite, update and deactivate
chunks.doc_title: Nimbus Gateway REST API v2 reference
chunks.heading: Deprecation of the earlier API
chunks.text: If the header appears, that call is going to the old API and needs to be updated. A practical migration usually follows this order. First, inventory every script, plugin and scheduled job that talks to Nimbus Gateway. Second, search your captured responses for the Deprecation header to identify which of them still use the old endpoints. Third, change each one to the current base URL and review its requests against this reference, paying attention to authentication, pagination and error handling, since these conventions may differ from what you built originally. Finally, test in a non-production workspace before switching over. Once everything you own is calling the current API, remove the old credentials and configuration so nothing is left pointing at endpoints that are going away.

briefs: Files resource: upload, download and metadata fields
Users resource: invite, update and deactivate
chunks.doc_title: Nimbus Gateway REST API v2 reference
chunks.heading: Files resource: upload, download and metadata
chunks.text: The files resource lets you add content to your workspace, retrieve it again and read or change the information that describes it. Every call is made beneath the base URL and authenticated with your Authorization header. To upload a file, send a POST request to /files. Include the destination folder, the file name and the content itself. If your tool supports it, use a multipart request so the descriptive fields and the file contents travel together. When the upload succeeds, the response returns the new file object, including its identifier, which you should store because every later operation refers to it.

briefs: Files resource: upload, download and metadata fields
Users resource: invite, update and deactivate
chunks.doc_title: Nimbus Gateway REST API v2 reference
chunks.heading: Files resource: upload, download and metadata
chunks.text: If a file with the same name already exists in the folder, the API reports a conflict instead of silently replacing it, so decide in your code whether to rename or update. To download a file, send a GET request to the file's content path using its identifier. The response streams the raw content rather than a JSON document, so write it directly to disk instead of parsing it. Check the status of the response before saving anything. Metadata is returned whenever you fetch a file object. Typical fields include the identifier, name, parent folder, content type, owner, created and modified timestamps, and a description. To change a name, move a file to another folder or edit its description, send a PATCH request containing only the fields you want to change. Fields you leave out remain as they were.

briefs: Files resource: upload, download and metadata fields
Users resource: invite, update and deactivate
chunks.doc_title: Nimbus Gateway REST API v2 reference
chunks.heading: Users resource: invite, update and deactivate
chunks.text: The users resource lets administrators manage the people who have access to a workspace. These calls require a credential that belongs to an account with administrative rights, otherwise the API will refuse them. To invite someone, send a POST request to /users with their email address and the role you want them to have. Nimbus sends them an invitation message, and the new user object is returned immediately with a status showing that the invitation is pending. If the person is already a member, the API tells you so rather than creating a duplicate. You can resend an invitation later by repeating the request for that address.

briefs: Files resource: upload, download and metadata fields
Users resource: invite, update and deactivate
chunks.doc_title: Nimbus Gateway REST API v2 reference
chunks.heading: Users resource: invite, update and deactivate
chunks.text: To update a user, send a PATCH request to that user's path, using the identifier from the user object. Include only the fields you want to change, such as the display name, the role or the team they belong to. Anything you omit stays the same. After the call, read the returned object to confirm the change took effect, especially when you are adjusting roles, since these affect what the person can see. To deactivate a user, send a DELETE request to the same path, or set the status field to inactive if you prefer to use an update.
